_about: Extra glossary terms (beyond each lesson's Definitions section) plus search aliases. Edit freely; run build.py to regenerate.

terms.def: The ability to understand a system's health, performance, and behavior from the inside out, using connected data so problems can be explained and acted on, not just detected.
Metrics, logs, and traces. Each gives insight alone; together they tell the full story. Dynatrace captures all three automatically.
Event data Dynatrace captures beyond metrics, logs, and traces, giving extra context about an application's behavior and changes.

The most complete OneAgent monitoring mode and the recommended default: host and process metrics plus traces and profiling from the service layer. Opt-in features include log management and application security.
OneAgent mode that collects host and process metrics but no service-layer tracing or profiling. Common for database servers.
The lightest OneAgent mode: essential host metrics plus topology and host-criticality data. Logs and advanced features are off by default. Suited to kiosks, POS terminals, and inventorying hosts.
A ready-to-use Dynatrace App that ships with the platform, such as apps for analyzing user sessions, service performance, or logs (e.g. Infrastructure & Operations, Problems).
A Dynatrace App your team builds to meet specific business or technical needs. It runs inside the Dynatrace platform.
A data store combining a data lake's scale with a warehouse's structure. Dynatrace describes Grail as a causational data lakehouse.
The bottom Smartscape layer: the physical or virtual locations where hosts run.
An interaction between a user and a web application that triggers a request to a web server, such as clicking a login button. Dynatrace tracks its performance, errors, and experience.
A user action in which a full page loads, such as opening the home page, login page, or search results.
A user action where part of a page updates without a full reload (an XMLHttpRequest), such as applying a filter or clicking "Next" in a gallery.
A user action Dynatrace doesn't capture by default that you define yourself with the Dynatrace JavaScript API (or OpenKit for thick clients), such as tracking PDF downloads.
The default application that collects all web traffic until detection rules route it into specific applications. Older traffic stays here after rules are added.
Insight into what happens inside a request down to methods and database queries — for example, which method took the most time or which SQL statement was slow.
Real User Monitoring for iOS and Android apps. Captures load times, errors, Apdex, and app crashes, and tracks touch interactions instead of clicks. Uses its own instrumentation setup.
The share of requests or actions that fail, such as broken images, 404 Page Not Found, or 500/503 server errors. Errors make an action "frustrated" in Apdex regardless of speed.
A synthetic monitor that loads a single page (e.g. a home or login page) on a schedule for basic uptime and performance checks.
A synthetic monitor that replays a multi-step user journey (log in → search → purchase). Recorded with the Dynatrace Synthetic Recorder Chrome extension.
A synthetic monitor that calls an API endpoint or URL without loading a visual page — a scheduled "are you there?" check, like ping or curl.
A breakdown of the loading sequence of a page's resources (scripts, images, CSS) that shows what slowed a user action. Based on W3C timing standards.
Labeling user sessions with an identifier such as a username or email (e.g. picking up "Ryan" from a "Welcome Ryan" element) to connect behavior to specific users.
A Dynatrace JavaScript API call that ends the current user session on demand, for example when a user logs out.
The share of sessions with only one action before the user leaves, often caused by slow loads or a poor experience. Bounce sessions usually don't consume a license.
The most severe problem type: something is unreachable, such as a host or a synthetic monitor being unavailable.
The second most severe problem type: rising error rates or application failures.
The third most severe problem type: performance degradation, such as a page or service responding more slowly than its baseline.
The fourth most severe problem type: infrastructure strain such as high CPU or memory usage.
A user-defined problem based on specific business needs. It can be set to any severity, or to the "custom" severity, which is the lowest.
The setting that controls how alerts are delivered — email, Slack, PagerDuty, or other channels. Workflows can also send them.
Settings that tune when and how anomalies are triggered. They can be set globally or per entity.
A problem-analysis tool for pinpointing spikes in application errors. The first tool to reach for when a problem involves errors.
A problem-analysis tool that highlights which services or methods are causing a slowdown. The first tool to reach for with slowdowns.
A tool that breaks a request down across every service it touches, showing where delays occur.
A problem-analysis tool showing which users were affected by a problem and how.
A Dynatrace Intelligence capability that creates auto-adaptive thresholds and learns seasonal (time-of-day, day-of-week) behavior of metrics.
A Dynatrace Intelligence capability used in dashboards and notebooks to predict future values of a metric.
The Dynatrace Intelligence capability that detects anomalies, determines root causes, groups related problems, and understands system topology.
An analysis view mentioned in the course for slicing data across several dimensions at once to find patterns.
A prebuilt public app from the Dynatrace Hub for learning and practising DQL.
A Hub extension that tells OneAgent (or an ActiveGate, remotely) to collect extra metrics for a specific technology such as Tomcat or Kafka, usually with a pre-made dashboard.
Automatically hiding sensitive data such as tokens, API keys, or sensitive code information while logs are ingested.
Dynatrace's runtime security capability: it watches code while it runs to flag vulnerable third-party libraries and block live attacks.
The Application Security capability that flags known vulnerabilities in third-party libraries and frameworks actually used at runtime.
The Application Security capability that blocks real-time attacks such as SQL injection.
Dynatrace's security partner whose vulnerability data, combined with Dynatrace Intelligence's topology knowledge, is used to calculate the DSS.
One timed operation within a trace (for example, a single method or service call). OpenTelemetry lets you add custom spans, and business events can extract values from spans.

A platform for running containerized applications at scale. In the course's food-truck analogy: containers are workers, pods are trucks, nodes are the lot, and the cluster is the whole festival. Monitored by the Dynatrace Operator.
A small, focused unit that runs one specific process with just what it needs. In Kubernetes, containers live inside pods.
The Kubernetes unit that wraps one or more containers — the "food truck" in the course analogy.
A Kubernetes machine that hosts many pods — the "food-truck lot" in the course analogy.
A group of Kubernetes nodes working together to run applications — the whole "food festival" in the course analogy.
